institutionName: UiT The Arctic University of Norway

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer:
*I WENT TO UNIS ON SVALBARD, AND NOT TO TROMSØ AT UIT* 
The academic opportunity is also a big reason, as UNiS is natural science only facility and conducts specialised Arctic research. 
But the biggest reason was for the nature and for the unique experience of living in the high Arctic.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I'm not sure... It had to be financially feasible, so the Erasmus grant was a nice addition. But a crucial aspect was that everyday life had to include nature and adventure. You can get this in other places than Svalbard, but I felt I could always go to these other places. It's a unique opportunity to live on Svalbard for that period of time. Being a tourist for a few days is a whole other world than actually living there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It was unreal. Again, this is the UNIS on Svalbard so I have no idea how it is at Tromsø.
The overall study experience was amazing. However, it does require the person to take initiative. Not necessarily to make friends, but to go out on adventures. It can be hard, logistically, on Svalbard and sometimes you have to get creative. Seek help from the residents, like burrowing a car, find a boat to fix, take som (well-assessed) risks... You will go on some amazing field trips with the course (so much money pumped into this uni) so you will also get cool experiences without taking any initiative. 
Living and studying here is not for everyone. If you don't like the cold, hiking and being outside doing type 2&3 fun, it's not the place for you. I think you can find other places where the town/city and indoor life is a lot more fun and cozy.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: A lot of assistance. It's such a small place and every student lives in the same accommodation. UNIS is very good at introducing you to the island.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
You live at Elvesletta dorm. here you are guaranteed housing if you're enrolled as a student. Every other student lives here so pretty easy. You have your own room with your own toilet and shower. Kitchen is shared between approx. 7 other students. 
*FYI they are very open to comments regarding housing. so if you want to stay in the same kitchen as a friend it's very possible. You can even put a note that you want the good view (one side of the building) on x level of the building.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: You go buy food from the supermarket and cook it up in the shared kitchen.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
*FYI they are very open to comments regarding housing. so if you want to stay in the same kitchen as a friend it's very possible. You can even put a note that you want the good view (one side of the building) on x level of the building. 
It's a nice place to live, but as everywhere else you can be "unlucky" to be in a boring/dirty kitchen. Here, it is possible to change kitchen or just spend your time at another kitchen with your actual friends. 
The rent is around 4050 DKK per month. I think that's including electricity, water, heating etc. 
Some of the food prices are ridiculous but an easy way to get around this is not to buy these foods... Eggs are actually cheaper than here in Denmark. Just buy the cheap stuff and you can spend around the same money as back in Denmark.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing is new and "high-tech". super nice.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It is actually very confusing. So basically: you are not going on exchange to svalbard. You are going on exchange to a partner university (like Tromsø, Oslo etc.) The partner uni doesn't matter. But through this partner university you're taking the courses which are on Svalbard. This also means that you only know that you're going to Svalbard much later and that there is a risk that you "have to" stay at the partner university if you don't get offered a spot on the courses that take place on Svalbard. In that way, it's actually a bit of a risk doing this, say that you really don't want to spend a semester at Oslo and now it's too late to change to Canada or whatever. The good news is that it's relatively "easy" getting in on the autumn semester as this is not skiing/snowscooter season. I think, if your average is above 7 you have a chance. If it's above 9 you will get a spot. (take this with a grain of salt, but this is how It sounds from who I've talked to). 
It's worth being on the waiting list as well as a lot of people jump ship.
Now the spring semester is a lot harder as more Norwegians apply (they have quotas from the partner universities that they gets priority). I got in on the spring semester by being on the waiting list. This is with an average of 10,2. So it's relatively hard. Another way is doing your bachelor's thesis or even a PUK project here. The professors are very open to this.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
See above. 
In addition you use their own portal to apply for the UNIS courses. You send in some documents and information and they usually get back to you 2 weeks after the deadline.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not really a lot. A lot of emailing back and forth in which they are helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I got the courses I wanted (and the only ones available). 
AB-201: Arctic terrestrial biology
AB-204: Arctic population ecology

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember the deadlines and don't be afraid to email them.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The courses were super cool. it is very different from Copenhagen university in that they focus on applied biology rather than theoretical. This means LOTS of fieldwork. LOTS of guest lecturers from around the world, and LOTS of scientific articles to be read. There isn't really a book as curriculum. Just articles and the slides that the teachers goes through. There is also some big assignments like a group report and posters.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level wasn't that hard. I would almost say it was easier than back at Copenhagen but that's also wrong as it's so different. I definelty prefer the UNIS way, but the exams are much harder at Copenhagen. At the same time the project and poster stuff I had never done back home so this scientific writing was hard for me.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Applied biology vs theoretical. That's UNIS' whole thing. The field work was amazing. We went to Ny-Ålesund (79 degrees) in a twin otter, for a week. This was an insane (and expensive for UNIS) trip. Saw lots of polar bears and Arctic foxes. 
There is also no big seminars. the teaching is VERY intimate. Small classroom style and you're even friends with the teacher. Very different from the boring teaching elsewhere.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
AB-201: Arctic terrestrial biology
AB-204: Arctic population ecology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I am a marine biologist at heart, so the AB-201 could at times be boring. But it was actually more about the Arctic in general which was still cool. 
AB-204 is mostly marine biology ecology tbh.

Food DKK per month *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Sooooo much gear. There's a lot of gear to buy if you don't already own it. Spikes for the shoes, sleeping mat, sleeping bag etc etc. 
There is however an organization called student equipment where you can burrow (free) a lot of the essentials. 
The 300 for transportation is because I rented a bike from the university. this is optional and lots of people didnt.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Eggs were less expensive. I was surprised by how cheap everything is after all you heard about Svalbard and the Arctic. but I think that's because everything in Denmark is already so expensive. 
Snowscooters are cheaper than I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I didn't really participate in the clubs, but I know there is kayak-polo, indoor football, skiing/ ice hockey in the spring, and so on. 
I was part of the diving club which is pretty dead at the moment. I did dive however and that was cool. 
I'm planning to try to start the diving club again for both free diving and scuba diving. Then you have the nature and the cabins which of course is where it's at.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go out in nature and sleep in the cabins. Spend some money for a cruise to Pyramiden. hike to Grumant. If you can find a boat, then go to Barentsburg. Explore the mountains. 
If you have a camera, go out and find the Arctic fox and reindeer.
The university also owns a student cabin. Very cozy. Got to the Nordenskjold cabin. Go to the mines. Early in the season, go whale watching.

If you manage to burrow/buy a boat then go fishing and explore the fjords!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Lots of knitting if that's your thing. Some small cafes. There's great concerts. There's really good restaurants (pricey). And then of course the friday gathering and afterparties at Elvesletta afterwards.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Culture wise it's mostly norwegian. Climate wise, it takes some time.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: There are no local students. Everyone are guests and therefore looking for friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing really. Mostly just the abundance of knitting and love for hiking/nature is different from Denmark

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Love for nature.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Beware that the stay peaks early. As in all the cool activities and field works is in the first half of the stay. It gets totally dark by 12th of November but already around mid October it's pretty dark. This can take a mental toll on some people. There is still things to do but not as much. Mostly skiing and ice caving in November and December. 
2. Be aware of the unique application method for these courses in contrary to other exchange places. Read above for more.
3. Look into buying a boat with a friend or something. it really is worth it!
Also some people applied for grants and got a lot of money despite already having the Erasmus. might be worth looking into.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think I've covered all of it in the above answers.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The animals and nature.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing school with social/outdoor life.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
